title: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence
pub: Science, vol. 381, no. 6654, pp. 187-192 (14 July 2023), DOI 10.1126/science.adh2586; OA working-paper version: MIT (2 March 2023)
author: Shakked Noy · Whitney Zhang

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source materially strengthens the cluster’s core proposition with randomized evidence that generative AI can improve speed and quality on bounded professional-writing tasks while sharply reallocating effort from drafting to editing. Its external-validity caveat—especially the absence of context-specific knowledge—and its restraint about longer-run labour effects reinforce the cluster’s distinction between task-level gains and general competence or organisational value.
qs: Our results show that ChatGPT substantially raises average productivity: time taken       decreases by 0.8 SDs and output quality rises by 0.4 SDs.
Post-treatment, the share of time spent writing a rough draft falls by more than half and the share of time spent editing more than doubles.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source directly supports the distinction between assisted task performance and career outcomes: it finds substantial speed and quality gains, including narrower performance gaps, but treats reduced labour demand and adverse distributional effects as possibilities rather than demonstrated employment or income outcomes.
qs: Our results show that ChatGPT substantially raises average productivity: time taken       decreases by 0.8 SDs and output quality rises by 0.4 SDs.

The experimental evidence suggests that ChatGPT largely substitutes for worker effort rather than complementing workers’ skills, potentially causing a decrease in demand for workers, with adverse distributional effects as capital owners gain at the expense of workers.

st.t: Impact measurement: Sample balance does not remove attrition
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s methodological framing: it presents treatment–control means and occupational composition as descriptive checks, while not treating those comparisons as evidence of an AI productivity effect. It also supports the narrower finding of broadly similar first-task averages across groups.
qs: The right-hand side column shows the difference in means between treatment and control (levels of significance: ∗ 10%, ∗∗ 5%, and ∗∗∗ 1%).

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction between task-level gains and broader outcomes: it finds faster, higher-quality performance on bounded professional-writing tasks, while warning that short, context-light tasks may overstate usefulness and cannot establish whole-job or labor-market effects. It also supports the cluster’s claims about narrowing performance gaps and task redistribution, but does not provide evidence on durable skill formation.
qs: Our results show that ChatGPT substantially raises average productivity: time taken       decreases by 0.8 SDs and output quality rises by 0.4 SDs.
First, the tasks are relatively short, self-contained, and lack a dimension of context-specific knowledge, which may inflate our estimates of ChatGPT’s usefulness.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The randomized experiment supports the cluster’s central claims that generative AI can deliver substantial but bounded productivity gains, restructure task composition, and disproportionately assist lower-performing users. Its short, context-light writing tasks and partial-equilibrium design also reinforce the cluster’s caution that task-level results do not establish general professional autonomy or labour-market displacement. It does not directly address legal verification or apprenticeship risks.
qs: Our results show that ChatGPT substantially raises average productivity: time taken       decreases by 0.8 SDs and output quality rises by 0.4 SDs.
First, the tasks are relatively short, self-contained, and lack a dimension of context-specific knowledge, which may inflate our estimates of ChatGPT’s usefulness.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on measuring practical productivity through task outputs, time, attitudes, baseline performance and observed tool use rather than inferring gains from adoption. Its selective-attrition checks also reinforce the cluster’s concern with causal qualifications. However, the excerpt reports uptake and methods, not productivity-effect estimates, so it does not establish whether AI saved or consumed time.
qs: We collect participants’ output and elicit total time taken, time taken on various subcom- ponents of the task, job satisfaction, self-efficacy, and beliefs about automation.
The attrition rate is 5% in the control group and 10% in the treatment group.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source supports the cluster by documenting substantial productivity gains in a specific, bounded workflow—mid-level professional writing—and larger benefits for lower-ability workers. Its task-specific experimental scope provides evidence for equalization under some conditions, without establishing that weaker users always benefit most across tasks or that narrower productivity gaps translate into broader economic equality.
qs: Our results show that ChatGPT substantially raises average productivity: time taken       decreases by 0.8 SDs and output quality rises by 0.4 SDs.
Inequality between workers       decreases, as ChatGPT compresses the productivity distribution by benefiting low-ability       workers more.

kp.k: Randomized experiment tests professional writing, not legal work
kp.d: The supplied body identifies itself as a 2 March 2023 working paper, not peer reviewed, although the document header also cites the subsequent Science publication. Its preregistered online experiment involves 444 experienced, college-educated professionals completing two incentivized, occupation-specific writing tasks lasting 20–30 minutes. Half were randomly introduced to ChatGPT between tasks; controls signed up for Overleaf. Three blinded occupational professionals evaluated each output, with an average cross-evaluator correlation of 0.44. The studied occupations do not include lawyers.
qs: Working Paper (not peer reviewed)
In an online experiment, we recruit 444 experienced, college-educated professionals and assign each to complete two occupation-specific, incentivized writing tasks.
The occupations we draw on are marketers, grant writers, consultants, data analysts, human resource professionals, and managers.
Quality is assessed by (blinded) experienced professionals working in the same occupations.

kp.k: High treatment uptake accompanies some control-group usage
kp.d: Among treated participants, 92% successfully signed up and 81% used ChatGPT on the second task, rating usefulness 4.4 out of 5. Before treatment, approximately 70% had heard of ChatGPT and 30% had used it. Control-group usage of 10–20% left an experimentally induced usage gap of at least 60 percentage points. The authors interpret control usage as making their estimates lower bounds on usage effects. Attrition was 5% in controls and 10% in treatment; they report robustness checks addressing selective attrition.
qs: In the treatment group, 92% of treated participants successfully sign up for ChatGPT
81% choose to use it on the second task, giving it an average self-assessed usefulness score of 4.4 out of 5.
The fact that some control participants are using the tool means our estimates provide lower bounds on the effects of ChatGPT usage on productivity.
The attrition rate is 5% in the control group and 10% in the treatment group.

kp.k: ChatGPT reduces completion time while improving assessed quality
kp.d: The intervention reduced post-treatment task time by 10 minutes, or 37%, relative to controls' 27-minute average. Evaluator grades increased by 0.45 standard deviations, with similar gains in overall quality, writing quality, content quality and originality. Both effects are reported with p = 0.000. The authors describe shifts across the time and grade distributions rather than gains confined to narrow subgroups. Results were virtually identical under the linear and convex incentive schemes covering 80% of respondents.
qs: We measure productivity as earnings per minute.
In the treatment group, time taken on the post-treatment task drops by 10 minutes (37%) relative to the control group, who take an average of 27 minutes (p = 0.000).

Average evaluator grades in the treatment group increase by 0.45 standard deviations (p = 0.000), with roughly similar increases for overall grades and specific grades for writing quality, content quality, and originality.

kp.k: Supplementary interventions probe quality gains beyond time savings
kp.d: In an arm covering 20% of participants, both groups had exactly 15 minutes per task. Grades increased by 0.39 standard deviations, but the estimate was imprecise (p = 0.13) and had a slight baseline imbalance. Separately, 30% of treated participants could revisit their first response using ChatGPT: 23% replaced it and 25% edited it. The authors interpret these choices as suggesting participants valued quality improvement as well as speed.
qs: This holds effort fixed across the treatment and control groups, allowing us to interpret any difference in grades as a pure effect of ChatGPT access on productive capacity.

23% choose to replace their response with ChatGPT’s output and 25% use ChatGPT to edit their original response, suggesting that participants view ChatGPT as a way to improve output quality in addition to a convenient way to save time.

kp.k: Lower baseline performers gain more, compressing productivity differences
kp.d: Baseline ability is measured through first-task performance, not occupational seniority. Lower-scoring treated workers improved grades and reduced time, whereas higher-scoring workers maintained quality while becoming faster. The relationship between first- and second-task grades fell from 0.49 in controls to 0.25 in treatment, with p = 0.004 for the difference in slopes. The authors characterize this as initial inequalities being half-erased within the experimental tasks, not as evidence of reduced wage inequality.
qs: In the treatment group, initial inequalities are half-erased by the treatment: the correlation between first-task and second-task grades is only 0.25 (p-value on difference in slopes = 0.004).
This reduction in inequality is driven by the fact that participants who scored lower on the first round benefit more from ChatGPT access

kp.k: Observed gains primarily substitute for worker effort
kp.d: The authors distinguish direct submission of satisfactory AI output from human–AI complementarity that improves output through prompting or editing. They find little evidence for the latter: 68% of treated participants reported submitting initial ChatGPT output unedited, and participants were active for only three minutes on average after first pasting substantial text. Post-paste activity was uncorrelated with grades, and treated submissions did not outperform raw ChatGPT output. These findings concern the experiment's writing tasks, including its stronger quality-incentive arm.
qs: We observe neither of these pieces of evidence, suggesting that ChatGPT is increasing productivity primarily by substituting for worker effort.
68% of treated participants report submitting ChatGPT’s initial output without editing it
respondents do not receive higher average grades than raw ChatGPT output that we give to evaluators to grade, meaning we find no evidence that human editing is improving the ChatGPT output.

kp.k: Writing time shifts away from rough drafting
kp.d: Before treatment, participants allocated approximately 25% of their time to brainstorming, 50% to rough drafting and 25% to editing. After treatment, drafting's share fell by more than half and editing's share more than doubled. These are changes in time shares, alongside the overall reduction in task time.
qs: prior to the treatment, participants spend about 25% of their time brainstorming, 50% writing a rough draft, and 25% editing.
Post-treatment, the share of time spent writing a rough draft falls by more than half and the share of time spent editing more than doubles.

kp.k: Relative writing weakness does not predict greater benefits
kp.d: The authors test whether people whose writing is weak relative to their other skills benefit disproportionately, potentially expanding occupational opportunities. Neither self-ranked communication skills nor evaluator-based relative writing scores clearly predict willingness to pay or grade gains. Hypothetical monthly willingness to pay was approximately 0.5% of monthly salary across writing-skill groups. This null finding concerns relative skill profiles, distinct from the stronger gains among low baseline performers overall.
qs: We find no clear evidence for the aforementioned hypothesis.
respondents, regardless of their writing skills, are willing to pay about 0.5% of their monthly salary for a monthly subscription to ChatGPT.
people with comparatively poor writing skills do not experience unusually large grade gains.

kp.k: Immediate task satisfaction improves; self-efficacy evidence is weaker
kp.d: Section 2.7 reports task satisfaction rising by about 0.40 standard deviations (p = 0.000), whereas Figure 4 labels the effect 0.5 standard deviations. Self-efficacy rose by 0.20 standard deviations but imprecisely (p = 0.060). These measures capture enjoyment and perceived effectiveness during the assigned task, rather than durable attitudes toward participants' whole jobs.
qs: Figure 4 Panel (a) shows that ChatGPT substantially increases job satisfaction, by about 0.40 standard deviations (p = 0.000).
Panel B shows that it mildly and imprecisely increases self-efficacy, by 0.20 standard deviations (p = 0.060)
The results on job satisfaction and self-efficacy are similarly limited, reflecting enjoyment of a small task rather than feelings about a worker’s whole job

kp.k: Exposure increases both automation concerns and optimism
kp.d: After the second task, treated participants expressed greater worry about occupational replacement, greater excitement about productivity enhancement and greater overall optimism about AI. Reported effects were respectively 0.26 standard deviations (p = 0.006), 0.39 (p = 0.000) and approximately 0.20 (p = 0.037). These are measured belief changes following exposure, not evidence that replacement or aggregate enhancement occurred.
qs: worry about automation increases by 0.26 standard deviations (p = 0.006), excitement by 0.39 (p = 0.000), and net optimism increases by about 0.20 (p = 0.037).

kp.k: Two-week follow-up finds increased workplace adoption
kp.d: The follow-up was still ongoing: 423 respondents had been invited, with an 82% response rate and no detected differential response by treatment. Past-week workplace use was 33% among treated participants versus 18% among controls. Among prior nonusers, the corresponding figures were 26% and 9% (p = 0.048). Users rated usefulness 3.65/5.00, below the experiment's rating; the authors suggest longer, more complex real tasks explain the difference. Overall job satisfaction did not differ between groups.
qs: This followup is still in progress, with an 82% response rate among the 423 respondents who have been invited so far, and no evidence of differential response rates by treatment status.
33% of former treatment group participants have used ChatGPT in their job in the past week, relative to 18% of control group participants.
There is no difference between the former treatment and control in their overall satisfaction with their job in the followup survey.

kp.k: Context-specific knowledge limits applicability to real work
kp.d: Follow-up nonusers mostly reported that ChatGPT lacked the customer-, company- or real-time information needed for their writing. The authors acknowledge that short, self-contained experimental assignments omit much of this knowledge and may therefore inflate estimated usefulness. Workplace adoption supports practical value for some tasks but does not eliminate this limitation.
qs: Respondents who are not using ChatGPT in their jobs mostly report that this is because the chatbot lacks context-specific knowledge that forms an important part of their writing.
First, the tasks are relatively short, self-contained, and lack a dimension of context-specific knowledge, which may inflate our estimates of ChatGPT’s usefulness.

kp.k: Employment and distributional consequences remain conditional predictions
kp.d: The discussion suggests that effort substitution could reduce worker demand and shift gains toward capital owners. The introduction also considers a contrasting scenario in which cheaper, more productive services expand demand, employment and wages. Neither aggregate outcome is measured: the experiment captures immediate effects in selected occupations, while indirect adaptations and differences across occupations, tasks and skill levels remain unresolved.
qs: potentially causing a decrease in demand for workers, with adverse distributional effects as capital owners gain at the expense of workers.
In this case, demand for these services could expand, resulting in higher employment and wages as well as greater productivity for companies and cheaper products for consumers.
Second, an experiment, by its nature, captures only direct, immediate effects of ChatGPT on the selected occupations.
Only time and future research will fully reveal how ChatGPT and its successors will affect labor markets.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Noy and Zhang find that ChatGPT increases productivity and compresses performance differences in mid-level professional writing, primarily by substituting for worker effort; wider employment effects remain predictions.
pts.d: In the supplied March 2, 2023 working-paper text, the authors report a 10-minute (37%) reduction in task time and a 0.45-standard-deviation increase in evaluator grades. Lower-baseline performers improve quality and reduce time, while higher-baseline performers maintain quality and become faster. The authors interpret limited editing and the absence of a grade advantage over raw ChatGPT output as evidence of effort substitution rather than skill complementarity in these tasks. Rough-drafting's share of task time falls by more than half and editing's share more than doubles; these are changes in shares, not necessarily increases in absolute editing time. They find no clear evidence that comparatively weak writing skills, relative to other skills, predict greater benefits. Task enjoyment increases, while the self-efficacy estimate is positive but imprecise. Exposure increases both concern about replacement and enthusiasm about productivity enhancement. The discussion raises a possible decline in labour demand and redistribution toward capital owners, rather than reporting observed job displacement. The introduction also presents expansion of demand, employment and wages as an alternative conditional scenario.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on a preregistered randomized writing experiment, evaluator grades, task-process observations, self-reports and an incomplete two-week follow-up; employment predictions are not directly tested.
pts.d: The authors recruited 444 experienced, college-educated professionals for two incentivized, occupation-specific writing tasks. Half were randomly instructed to sign up for ChatGPT between tasks; controls signed up for Overleaf. Three blinded occupational professionals assessed each output. First-task performance provided a baseline measure for performance-distribution analysis. Minute-by-minute output snapshots supplemented reported time and helped detect tool use. Treatment-group uptake was 81%, with 10–20% control usage; the authors characterize their estimates as lower bounds on effects of usage. The baseline-to-second-task grade relationship falls from approximately 0.49 in controls to 0.25 in treatment, with p = 0.004 for the slope difference. Effort-substitution evidence includes 68% reporting submission of initial ChatGPT output without editing and about three minutes of activity after pasting text. A fixed-15-minute experimental arm yields a positive but imprecise 0.39-SD quality estimate (p = 0.13). The ongoing follow-up reports workplace usage of 33% in treatment versus 18% in controls. The text reports task-enjoyment improvement of about 0.40 SD, whereas Figure 4 labels it 0.5 SD; self-efficacy rises 0.20 SD (p = 0.060). Replacement concern rises 0.26 SD, enhancement excitement 0.39 SD, and net optimism 0.20 SD. No wages, employment changes or capital-income transfers are measured.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Findings concern immediate effects on short, self-contained writing tasks and early adoption two weeks later, not established long-run labour-market outcomes.
pts.d: Although the document header identifies the later Science publication, the supplied body is explicitly the March 2, 2023 working paper, marked not peer reviewed; the extracted estimates belong to that text. Experimental assignments were designed to take 20–30 minutes and supplied the necessary context in their prompts. The authors caution that limited task complexity and context-specific knowledge requirements may inflate usefulness estimates. Follow-up was still underway, with an 82% response rate among 423 invitees, and workplace usefulness was lower than in the experiment. Nonusers commonly cited missing customer-, company- or real-time knowledge. Task-level enjoyment does not establish improved satisfaction with a whole job. The authors explicitly leave long-run employment and distributional effects unresolved because adaptation and general-equilibrium effects can reinforce or counteract immediate findings. Outcomes may differ by occupation, task and skill level.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is college-educated professionals in six nonlegal occupations; broader implications concern workers, employers, capital owners and consumers.
pts.d: Participants were marketers, grant writers, consultants, data analysts, HR professionals and managers completing press releases, short reports, analysis plans and delicate emails. Lower and higher ability refer to baseline performance on the experimental task, not seniority, credentials or occupational rank. Lower-baseline performers receive larger quality gains; time savings extend across baseline performance levels. The authors find no clear differential benefit based on writing skill relative to other skills. Their wider scenarios include replacement of some writers and employer wage-cost savings, or expanded service demand with higher employment and wages and cheaper products. These are conditional labour-market implications, not measured outcomes. The source does not study lawyers, law firms, legal clients or legal-service delivery, so its findings should remain attributed to professional writing rather than converted into legal-sector claims.
